description: We’re a team of Computer Engineering students from Yıldız Technical University.
summary: On a Mars mission a message to the flight surgeon takes many minutes each way, Earth reference ranges do not fit a body adapting to spaceflight, and astronauts are measured only periodically with separate devices. ARGUS is an offline-first web app that helps a crew measure, understand and act on their own health. Every reading is judged three ways: against the astronaut's own baseline, against space-adapted rules from NASA sources, and against Earth reference ranges, plus a data-quality check. The screen says which layer raised the flag and counts the concerns caught only by the personal baseline. ARGUS measures with what is on board: webcam pulse, a 3-minute reaction test modeled on NASA's Reaction Self-Test, an on-screen vision screening check and guided vital-sign entry. It tracks NOAA proton flux and a crew dose ledger against NASA-STD-3001 limits, and sends FHIR-style packets over a delayed Earth link. The crew is simulated; the space-weather data and your own measurements are real. ARGUS is a prototype, not a medical device.
details:
Live demo: https://feyruzsultanli.github.io/argus-crew-health/ (sign in with demo PIN 2026)

Repository: https://github.com/FeyruzSultanli/argus-crew-health

Team Dark Star: İsmail Cem Şahin, Feyruz Sultanli, Fikret Mammadov, Rahil Bagirov

WHAT IS REAL AND WHAT IS SIMULATED

The four crew members, their daily readings, the cabin sensors and the solar-storm replay are simulated, and the app labels them SIMULATED or REPLAY on every screen. Real: the NOAA proton flux, the NASA OSDR pre-flight blood values used as anchors, the published limits, and anything you measure yourself (camera pulse, reaction test, vision check, manual entry). ARGUS is a prototype, not a medical device.

1. THE PROBLEM

Long missions expose crews to five hazards NASA's Human Research Program has mapped: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment. Three facts make self-assessment on board an engineering problem, not a dashboard exercise.

- The doctor is minutes away. Between Earth and Mars a one-way message takes up to about 22 minutes, depending on where the planets are, so a question and its answer can take most of an hour. Deep-space missions mean more communication delay and less reliance on Earth. In our demo the crew is on day 143 of a Mars transit, with a modeled one-way delay of 11 minutes.

- Earth "normal" does not fit a body in space, and population ranges do not fit a person. In long-duration ISS crews, hematocrit measured 10–12 % higher (relative) than before flight, part of it a sample-handling artefact; resting core body temperature rose about 1.0 °C over about 2.5 months; and measured sleep averaged about 6.1 hours against 8.5 hours scheduled. Fixed thresholds either raise false alarms for these known adaptations or miss a change that is large for one person but still "within range".

- Astronauts are not monitored continuously. The ISS medical kit is a collection of discrete devices used to assess crew health periodically, and vital signs are recorded mainly during exercise and spacewalks. A crew needs low-burden ways to measure, ideally with hardware it already carries.

2. WHAT ARGUS DOES (FOUR PILLARS, AS BUILT)

A. Personal · Space · Earth verdict, plus data quality

Every health signal gets three independent judgements: is it unusual for this astronaut (personal baseline), is it expected or concerning in this mission environment (space rules from NASA standards and evidence), and would a clinic on Earth flag it (Earth reference ranges). A quality layer asks whether the reading can be trusted. The combined verdict is one of Nominal, Expected in space, Watch, Act or No data, and the screen always says which layer drove it. The headline counter is "Caught only by personal baseline". In the demo, flight engineer K. Osei's resting pulse is 69 bpm on day 143: normal for the Earth and space rules, but 11 beats above her own usual 58 bpm, so the personal layer says Act.

B. Measure with what is on board (Measurement Lab)

- Camera pulse: resting pulse from the laptop webcam in 30 seconds with the published POS remote-photoplethysmography method, on-device face tracking (MediaPipe Face Landmarker, self-hosted), and a quality score from five checks with plain-word reasons and an honest "retake" path. Video stays on the device; only the number is saved.

- Reaction Self-Test: a 3-minute psychomotor vigilance test modeled on NASA's PVT-B "Reaction Self-Test" (stimulus every 1–4 s, lapse at 355 ms or more), scored against the astronaut's own pre-flight lapses.

- Manual vitals with "how to measure" cards: blood pressure, heart rate, SpO2, temperature, glucose (mg/dL or mmol/L), body mass, sleep, mood and a symptom checklist; plus a two-tap quick check-in (mood, sleep, symptoms).

- Vision check, screening only (not a diagnosis), modeled on the ISS laptop vision tests: the screen is calibrated with a bank card; an Amsler grid per eye (20 × 20 squares of 5 mm) where the astronaut marks wavy, blurred or missing areas, compared with the previous test ("new area since last test"); and near acuity with a tumbling E at 60 cm. A new marked area gives Watch and a new square near the centre gives Act, through the existing vision rules and the in-flight exam schedule. The calibration is set by the user with a card and has not yet been checked independently with a ruler.

- Face fluid-shift scan, experimental and not validated: a 3-second scan measures cheek width, jaw width and eye opening relative to the distance between the pupils, from on-device face landmarks. No pre-flight scan exists in this demo, so the first scan on a device is the reference. Trend only: it never raises Watch or Act on its own, and no image is saved. It has not yet been tried on real faces.

- Coming next (not in this build): device import from wearables and dosimeters.

C. Radiation and environment awareness

- NOAA GOES proton flux (live, else the last cached copy, else a bundled snapshot, always with its age), converted to the NOAA S-scale (S1 at 10 pfu at ≥ 10 MeV).

- A crew dose ledger against the NASA-STD-3001 limits: career effective dose below 600 mSv, and below 250 mSv for the design solar particle event. Mars-cruise cosmic-ray dose uses the 1.8 mSv/day measured by Curiosity's RAD instrument on the way to Mars. Solar-event dose is modeled and labeled "Modeled — illustrative".

- A shelter advisory, labeled as a demo policy; real shelter calls come from the mission's radiation specialists.

- A solar-storm replay for the demo: a synthetic S2-class profile, always badged "REPLAY — synthetic, not a recorded event". No real event (≥ 10 pfu) occurred in the 7 days before the build, so nothing recorded was available to replay.

- Cabin CO2 against the NASA-STD-3001 1-hour limit of 3 mmHg and the 2.5 mmHg 7-day line that keeps headache risk below 1 %; cabin temperature and humidity against the standard's limits (simulated cabin sensors).

D. Built to plug into NASA

- Rules trace to NASA-STD-3001 items: V2 6004 (CO2), V1 4029 (ALARA), V1 4030 (career dose), V1 4031 (solar-event dose), V2 6012 / 6013 (temperature and humidity), V2 6109 (water).

- Export as a FHIR-style R4 Bundle (Patient + Observation, LOINC and UCUM codes, provenance, quality and verdict extensions) and as CSV.

- A delay-aware Earth link: the crew sends a compact packet to the flight surgeon, who sees it in a separate view only after the modeled delay ("arrives in 11 min (demo: 11 s)"), and can reply over the same delay.

- Architecture after NASA's Crew Health and Performance Integrated Data System Platform idea: one local crew health data service with source adapters and sinks.

Also on board: a clickable 3D body (HRA reference anatomy, male and female, with a 2D fallback), a mission-day scrubber that replays the timeline, trends with personal bands, a CMO crew overview, today's measurement plan with streaks, points, badges and a readiness index (demo), five protocols, and an offline handbook of 40 entries with a rule-based Ask box.

3. HOW IT WORKS

Three-layer verdict. Each signal is defined once (21 signals) with its personal-baseline settings, a space rule and an Earth rule. A pure TypeScript domain core evaluates the three layers and a quality layer, then combines them: a known spaceflight adaptation is downgraded to "Expected in space"; a poor-quality reading cannot raise Act; the result names the driving layer, the action and the source of every threshold.

Personal baseline statistics. For each astronaut and signal: a robust pre-flight reference (median and median absolute deviation with a spread floor), an adaptive in-flight reference over the last 14 days of normal readings, a robust z-score, a CuSum that accumulates smaller shifts over several days, and a small state machine with hysteresis so a single reading never raises Act. The same idea is published for wearables: resting heart rate compared with a personal baseline flagged infections before symptoms. No machine learning: there is no public in-flight vital-sign data to train on, and these statistics can be checked line by line.

Camera pulse pipeline. Webcam frames (640×480) → MediaPipe face landmarks → forehead and cheek regions → mean red, green and blue per frame → resampling to 30 Hz → POS projection → 0.7–3.0 Hz band-pass → Welch spectrum → pulse at the spectral peak, with five quality checks: signal-to-noise, consistency between the two halves of the 30-s window, head motion, lighting (including clipped pixels) and face presence. Processing runs in a web worker in memory; frames are never stored or sent.

Architecture. One local crew health data service sits in the middle.

- Into the service: NOAA GOES proton flux (live, cached or bundled snapshot); a seeded simulator, labeled SIMULATED, anchored on bundled NASA OSDR pre-flight blood values; and the Measurement Lab (camera pulse in a worker, Reaction Self-Test, vision check, experimental face scan, manual entry).

- Storage: IndexedDB, local and offline.

- Out of the service: the domain core (signals, rules, personal baseline, verdict, readiness), the crew and CMO screens, and the flight surgeon view, which receives a FHIR-style packet after the modeled delay.

Everything runs in the browser as an installable PWA. The network is needed only for live NOAA data; rules, baseline, measurements, 3D body and handbook work offline.

4. BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Earth-independent operations. The crew sees in seconds who needs attention, why, and the next step, without waiting for a ground loop that can take most of an hour on a Mars mission.

- Fewer false alarms, fewer misses. The space layer explains known adaptations (for example short in-flight sleep is "Expected in space"), and the personal layer catches changes that are large for one person but inside every population range.

- Hardware the crew already has. A laptop camera and screen replace extra devices for frequent, low-burden checks.

- On Earth too. The same personal-baseline approach applies to remote, rural or isolated care where a clinician is far away. Findings from space research already help with osteoporosis, cardiovascular disorders and type-2 diabetes on Earth.

- Standards-ready. NASA-STD-3001 traceability and a FHIR-style export make the output readable by a flight surgeon and by a future crew health data platform.

5. CREATIVITY AND WHAT WE CONSIDERED

What is creative. Most health dashboards compare a reading with one population range. ARGUS judges every reading three ways (personal baseline, space rules, Earth ranges) and shows which layer raised the flag, so the crew can see the concerns that only a personal baseline catches. It also turns hardware already on board into instruments: a laptop webcam measures pulse, and the screen runs a reaction test and a vision check. The Earth link is built around the communication delay instead of ignoring it.

What we considered.

- Honesty: every value is labeled real, simulated, modeled, demo or experimental, and a Limits page lists them.

- Safety: ARGUS never diagnoses or gives drug doses, and a poor-quality reading cannot raise Act.

- Privacy: camera video stays on the device; only the number is saved.

- Autonomy: everything except live NOAA data works offline.

- Crew burden: short, low-effort checks (30-second pulse, 3-minute reaction test, two-tap check-in).

- Traceability: every threshold links to a source, and rules trace to NASA-STD-3001 items.

- No machine learning: no public in-flight vital-sign data exists to train on, and the statistics can be checked line by line.

6. VALIDITY

- Sources registry. Every threshold, rate and limit on screen links to an entry in seed/sources.json with a status: verified (opened and checked at the source), partial (to be re-checked) or demo (our own parameter). Demo values show a "Demo parameter" tag. A test fails the build if the code cites a source id that is not in the registry.

- Independent verification. Every module is covered by automated tests. The personal baseline engine reproduces the ten test vectors of its specification exactly and agreed with an independent reference implementation on 600 random series (about 53,000 reading-days) with no disagreements. Radiation numbers (S-scale edges, dose ledgers, modeled solar-event dose, shelter table) were recomputed independently.

- Real data where it matters. Pre-flight blood values of the fictional crew are anchored on real, anonymised Inspiration4 measurements from NASA OSDR (OSD-569 blood counts, OSD-575 metabolic panel: 4 subjects × 3 pre-flight time points), with the dataset's own lab reference ranges.

- Camera pulse validation. The camera pulse has not yet been compared with a reference device; ARGUS shows a quality score and treats the result as a screening and trend value, not a clinical measurement.

- Honest limits, on screen. A Limits page lists what is real, measured, simulated, modeled, demo or experimental. The crew and their daily readings are simulated. The solar-storm replay is synthetic. The Mars-transit delay is a modeled demo profile, not derived from a trajectory. Readiness, demo band edges and baseline tuning constants are demo parameters. The vision check is screening only, and its screen calibration is set by the user with a bank card, not yet checked with a ruler. The face fluid-shift scan is experimental, not validated and trend only. The NASA DONKI event list is not connected (the service was unreachable on build day). ARGUS is a prototype, not a medical device: it never diagnoses or gives drug doses; its actions are re-measure, tell the Crew Medical Officer, send to the flight surgeon, or follow a listed protocol.

7. TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

TypeScript (strict), React 19, Vite 7, Tailwind CSS 4, React Router 7, Zustand, Dexie (IndexedDB), three.js with React Three Fiber and drei, Recharts, Motion, MediaPipe Tasks Vision (Face Landmarker, self-hosted WASM and model), vite-plugin-pwa (Workbox), Vitest, Testing Library, Playwright with axe-core, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages. Fonts IBM Plex (OFL), icons Lucide (ISC).

8. WHAT'S NEXT

- Paired validation of the camera pulse against a reference device, in several lighting conditions and skin tones.

- A ruler check of the vision-check calibration, and trials of the face fluid-shift scan on real faces.

- Device adapters for smart-garment and actigraphy files (Bio-Monitor- and ARCHeR-style) and dosimeter readings.

- Clinical review of every demo threshold and baseline constant with flight surgeons.

- Encryption at rest, real identity and access, and a connection to a CHP-IDSP-style data platform.
